stem: An NFL club's media team wants a 150-word recap in house style for every game. The input is always the same structured box-score JSON, and the steps never change: pick the key stats, draft the recap, check length and style. Which architecture best fits?

options.text: A code-driven prompt chain: one call drafts from the box score, then a programmatic gate checks length and style.
options.explanation: Correct. Every step is known in advance, so a workflow is cheaper, faster and easier to test than an agent, and the gate catches drafts that miss the format.

options.text: An autonomous agent with web search and file tools that decides for itself which steps each game recap needs.
options.explanation: Over-engineered. Model-driven control flow adds cost, latency and unpredictability to a task whose flowchart can be drawn before it starts.

options.text: A supervisor agent that hands stats, drafting and editing to three parallel subagents and then merges their output.
options.explanation: The steps depend on each other and the input is small, so splitting them across subagents adds coordination overhead and tokens without any benefit.

options.text: Two agents that critique and rewrite every recap in an open-ended loop until both of them agree it is ready to post.
options.explanation: An uncapped multi-agent debate is unpredictable and expensive. A deterministic length and style check is enough for clear, fixed criteria.

stem: A data platform team wants Claude to investigate failed nightly ETL jobs. Past failures were caused by expired credentials, upstream outages, schema changes and full disks, and each investigation took a different path depending on what the logs showed. Which design is the best fit?

options.text: A fixed prompt chain that always reads the logs, then the scheduler state, then the upstream status page, in that order.
options.explanation: A fixed order can't adapt when the first finding points somewhere else, and the stem says each investigation took a different path.

options.text: An agent loop with tools to read logs, query the scheduler and check upstream status, bounded by a turn cap.
options.explanation: Correct. The steps can't be known in advance and depend on what each tool reveals, which is what agents are for. The turn cap keeps the open-ended loop bounded.

options.text: A single model call that receives the last 100 lines of the failed job's log and returns a likely root cause.
options.explanation: One call over a fixed log slice can't check credentials, upstream services or disk state, so it misses causes outside those 100 lines.

options.text: A router that sorts each failure into one of three predefined categories and then runs that category's fixed script.
options.explanation: Routing works when the categories are known and stable. Here the failure modes are open-ended, so new causes would fall outside the predefined branches.

stem: A fantasy football platform wants an assistant that analyzes a user's roster and proposes trades with other league members. Once a trade is accepted by the league it cannot be reversed. Which design best addresses this constraint?

options.text: Give the agent the trade tool directly and add a system prompt line telling it to be careful before submitting trades.
options.explanation: A prompt asks but doesn't guarantee. With an irreversible action, a mistaken or injected trade still executes.

options.text: Use the most capable model available so that the agent's trade proposals are accurate enough to run without review.
options.explanation: A stronger model lowers the error rate but doesn't add a recovery path. The cost-of-error criterion asks whether mistakes can be caught, not just how rare they are.

options.text: Let the agent research and propose trades freely, but require explicit user approval before the trade tool executes.
options.explanation: Correct. The open-ended analysis suits an agent, while the irreversible step gets a human approval gate, so errors are caught before they cost anything.

options.text: Raise the agent's turn limit so it has room to double-check each trade on its own before it submits it to the league.
options.explanation: More self-review turns don't create an external check. The agent can still submit a wrong trade, and nothing stops it.

stem: In a scouting app built on the Agent SDK, a coach discusses a specific linebacker with the main agent for several turns. The main agent then delegates "check the latest injury report for the player we discussed" to a subagent, which returns a generic league-wide summary. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

options.text: The subagent's context window was too small to hold the discussion. Assign it a model with a larger context window.
options.explanation: Window size isn't the issue. The subagent never received the discussion at all, so a bigger window would still be empty of it.

options.text: The subagent ran on a different model than the parent. Set its model to inherit so it shares the parent's memory.
options.explanation: Inheriting the model changes which model runs, not what the subagent sees. Subagents never share the parent's conversation.

options.text: The subagent ran in the background. Make it run in the foreground so it can read the coach's earlier messages live.
options.explanation: Foreground or background only changes whether the parent waits for the report. Neither mode gives the subagent the parent's history.

options.text: Subagents don't see the parent's conversation. Write the player's name, team and sources into the task prompt.
options.explanation: Correct. A non-fork subagent sees only its own prompt and the delegation message, so every name, path and constraint must be written into the task.

stem: A procurement team is building an assistant that reviews 30 independent vendor contracts and produces one risk summary. An architect proposes a lead agent that hands each contract to its own subagent. Which TWO benefits justify this design? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Each contract is read in its own context window, so only a short risk report reaches the lead agent.
options.explanation: Correct. Context isolation keeps the full text of 30 contracts out of the lead's context, which only grows by the reports.

options.text: The contracts are independent, so subagents can review them in parallel and cut wall-clock time.
options.explanation: Correct. Independent subtasks can run concurrently and finish in roughly the time of the slowest one.

options.text: Subagents share the lead agent's memory, so the review criteria never need to be restated to them.
options.explanation: Subagents start with a fresh context. The review criteria must be passed in the delegation prompt or the subagent's own prompt.

options.text: Splitting the work across many agents lowers the total token spend compared with a single agent.
options.explanation: Multi-agent designs usually use more tokens in total, since each agent pays for its own prompt and reasoning. The benefits are isolation and speed.

options.text: Each subagent manages its own spend, so the overall query no longer needs any budget or concurrency limit.
options.explanation: Every layer multiplies cost. Spend, depth and concurrency still need caps across the whole tree.

stem: A stadium ticketing service gets three kinds of support requests: refunds, seat transfers and general venue questions. Each kind has a well-documented procedure, its own tools and its own policy text, and mixing them in one prompt has caused policy mix-ups. Which workflow pattern fits best?

options.text: Routing: classify each request first, then send it to a prompt and tool set built for that category.
options.explanation: Correct. Routing separates distinct, well-defined categories so each branch gets focused instructions and only the tools it needs, which fixes the policy mix-ups.

options.text: Orchestrator-workers: a central model breaks every request into subtasks at runtime and assigns workers.
options.explanation: Orchestrator-workers suits tasks whose subtasks can't be predicted. These categories and procedures are known in advance.

options.text: One autonomous agent that holds every tool and every policy, and decides on its own how to handle a request.
options.explanation: This keeps all policies in one context, which is the cause of the mix-ups, and adds agent overhead to procedural work.

options.text: Voting: three model calls answer every request independently and the majority response is sent back.
options.explanation: Voting raises confidence on a single judgment but triples cost and does nothing to separate the conflicting policies.

stem: A league's competition committee wants every proposed rule change checked for conflicts across its 400-page rulebook. Which sections a proposal touches can't be known until the proposal is read, and some proposals touch one section while others touch a dozen. Which pattern fits best?

options.text: Sectioning: always run five parallel workers, one for each of the rulebook's five main chapters, and merge them.
options.explanation: Fixed sectioning works when the split is known in advance. Here it wastes calls on irrelevant chapters and can't go deeper where many sections are affected.

options.text: Orchestrator-workers: a lead model reads the proposal, picks the affected sections at runtime and delegates them.
options.explanation: Correct. Orchestrator-workers is the pattern for subtasks that depend on the input and can't be predefined, and it scales from one section to many.

options.text: Prompt chaining: one call summarizes the proposal, a second checks the whole rulebook, and a third writes a memo.
options.explanation: A fixed chain would push the entire rulebook through one step, which bloats context and doesn't adapt the work to each proposal's scope.

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts a conflict report and a second critiques it until the report passes review.
options.explanation: Evaluator-optimizer refines an output against criteria. It doesn't solve the core problem of deciding which sections to examine.

stem: A marketing team generates short ad copy that must meet clear, checkable rules: a character limit, required brand terms and no unverifiable claims. First drafts usually break one rule, and a human editor can point out exactly which. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Set temperature to 0 on the generation call so that drafts become deterministic and stop breaking the rules.
options.explanation: Current models reject non-default sampling parameters, and determinism wouldn't make a draft follow the rules anyway.

options.text: Build a supervisor with five copywriter subagents that each write a draft, and have it pick the best of the five.
options.explanation: More parallel drafts don't guarantee one passes every rule, and the design multiplies cost without any feedback on what is wrong.

options.text: An evaluator-optimizer loop: one call drafts, another checks the rules and returns feedback, with an iteration cap.
options.explanation: Correct. The criteria are clear and the feedback is actionable, which is exactly when an evaluator-optimizer loop adds value. The cap keeps it bounded.

options.text: Turn the generator into an agent with web search so it can study competitor ads before it writes each draft.
options.explanation: Research doesn't address rule compliance. The failure is breaking checkable rules, which calls for an evaluation step, not more autonomy.

stem: An accounts-payable team needs vendor name, invoice date and total pulled from each uploaded PDF invoice into JSON. An engineer proposes a five-agent hierarchy with a planner, an extractor, two validators and a formatter. Which review comment is most appropriate?

options.text: Add a sixth agent as an arbiter, so the two validators have a tie-breaker whenever they disagree on a field.
options.explanation: This makes an already over-engineered design bigger. The task doesn't need multiple agents at all.

options.text: Replace the hierarchy with one autonomous agent holding file tools, so it can decide which fields to extract.
options.explanation: The fields are fixed, so the model doesn't need to decide anything. An agent loop is still more machinery than the task needs.

options.text: Keep the hierarchy but move the planner to a cheaper model, since planning is the least demanding of the roles.
options.explanation: This trims a little cost but keeps the unnecessary coordination, latency and failure points of five agents.

options.text: This is single-step extraction: one call with structured outputs plus a code check does the job for far less.
options.explanation: Correct. Start with the simplest tier that works. A single call with a schema handles fixed-field extraction, and code can validate the result.

stem: A team's analytics group wants to rename its core PlayEvent model and change its fields across the codebase. Each edit depends on decisions made in earlier edits, such as how a renamed field is mapped in serializers and tests. A developer proposes four parallel subagents, each editing a quarter of the files. What is the best response?

options.text: Use one agent working sequentially, because tightly coupled edits need shared context that parallel subagents lack.
options.explanation: Correct. When every step depends on what the others decided, splitting the work across isolated contexts produces conflicting choices. One agent is simpler and more consistent.

options.text: Keep the four subagents and raise the concurrency limit, so that all of them finish at about the same time.
options.explanation: Speed isn't the problem. Each subagent still makes its own mapping decisions without seeing the others.

options.text: Keep the four subagents but give each one the full conversation history of the other three as they work.
options.explanation: Subagents don't see each other's histories, and piping transcripts between them defeats the context isolation that justified them.

options.text: Run the four subagents twice each with voting, then keep whichever version of each file appears most often.
options.explanation: Voting multiplies cost and can't reconcile choices that are inconsistent across files. It treats a coordination problem as a confidence problem.

stem: A scouting department's Agent SDK app lets the main agent spawn subagents freely. One broad prompt grew into a deep tree of nested subagents, and that query's cost was many times the usual. Which change addresses this most directly?

options.text: Add a system prompt instruction asking the main agent to keep delegation to a minimum and watch its spending.
options.explanation: A prompt steers but doesn't enforce. The docs advise setting hard limits as well, because Claude decides on its own when to delegate.

options.text: Set a spend cap with maxBudgetUsd and limit subagent nesting depth and concurrency through the SDK settings.
options.explanation: Correct. The SDK enforces the spend cap across the whole tree, including subagents, and the depth and concurrency limits stop runaway fan-out.

options.text: Remove all subagent definitions and instead raise maxTurns, so that the main agent does every task itself.
options.explanation: This drops the isolation benefits, and the built-in general-purpose subagent can still be spawned. A higher turn cap also adds no spend limit.

options.text: Move the app to Managed Agents, where subagent threads are hosted by Anthropic and don't add token costs.
options.explanation: Hosting changes who runs the loop, not who pays for tokens. Every agent's tokens are still billed.

stem: An insurer is considering an autonomous agent to settle small property claims end to end. During discovery the team records five findings. Which TWO findings argue for staying with a workflow or a single call instead of an agent? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Every claim follows the same four documented steps, and the team has already drawn the full flowchart.
options.explanation: Correct. If the steps can be specified in advance, the complexity criterion isn't met, and a code-driven workflow is cheaper and more predictable.

options.text: Payouts are sent the moment a claim is approved, and there is no review step or way to reverse them.
options.explanation: Correct. When errors can't be caught or recovered, the cost-of-error criterion fails, so autonomy isn't appropriate without redesign.

options.text: Each settled claim saves several hours of adjuster time, which the business values highly.
options.explanation: High value supports an agent rather than arguing against it. Value is one of the criteria an agent must meet.

options.text: In internal evaluations, Claude handled similar document-review tasks with high accuracy.
options.explanation: This shows viability, which supports the agent option. It isn't a reason to stay with a simpler tier.

options.text: Each claim requires reading several documents, such as photos, estimates and a policy file.
options.explanation: Reading several inputs is compatible with any tier. On its own it doesn't argue against an agent.

stem: A sports network on Managed Agents designs a coordinator that delegates to section-editor agents, each of which is itself configured with a multiagent roster of fact-checker agents. Creating the coordinator agent fails with a validation error. Which explanation and fix are correct?

options.text: The roster lists too many agents at once. Split the section editors across two coordinators and run both in parallel.
options.explanation: The roster limit is generous, and the failure comes from nesting, not count. Two coordinators would hit the same rule.

options.text: The fact-checkers need their own sandboxes. Give each agent a separate environment so their threads don't collide.
options.explanation: Agents in a multiagent session share the session's sandbox and filesystem by design. Environments aren't the cause of a create error.

options.text: Delegation is only one level deep. Flatten it so the coordinator calls fact-checkers directly, or use a workflow run.
options.explanation: Correct. An agent that has its own multiagent configuration can't be listed as another agent's subagent. Flattening the roster or using a dynamic workflow fits the limit.

options.text: The nesting depth defaults to one level. Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH to 3 in the session environment.
options.explanation: That variable controls subagent depth in the Agent SDK and Claude Code, not Managed Agents. Managed Agents rejects the nested configuration itself.

stem: A draft-prep agent compares ten prospects, reading about 200 college game logs for each one. Running it as a single agent, the context fills with log text and its comparisons get vaguer as the run goes on. Which TWO changes best fix this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Give each prospect's log reading to a subagent that returns a short structured profile to the lead agent.
options.explanation: Correct. The logs stay in each subagent's own context, so the lead agent compares ten compact profiles instead of 2,000 raw logs.

options.text: Give the log-reading subagents read-only tools and a cheaper model, since the work is reading and summarizing.
options.explanation: Correct. Least-privilege tools reduce risk, and reading-heavy work is a good fit for a cheaper model, which offsets the extra agents' cost.

options.text: Pass the lead agent's full conversation into each subagent so every subagent has all of the scouting context.
options.explanation: This copies the bloat into every subagent. Pass only the task-specific instructions each subagent needs.

options.text: Have each subagent return its full transcript, so the lead agent can double-check every log the subagent read.
options.explanation: Returning transcripts puts the raw logs back into the lead's context and cancels the isolation benefit.

options.text: Keep a single agent but move it to a model with a larger context window so that all the logs still fit.
options.explanation: A bigger window raises the limit but doesn't stop recall degrading as irrelevant tokens pile up.

stem: A sportsbook must flag ads that could appeal to minors before they run. Missing a problem ad is very costly, and a single Claude check gives borderline ads inconsistent verdicts. The task is the same for every ad and needs no tools. Which pattern best fits?

options.text: An autonomous agent that researches each ad's audience on the web before deciding
options.explanation: The task is a fixed check with no tools needed. An agent adds cost and unpredictability without addressing inconsistency.

options.text: Routing, sending each ad to a different specialist prompt by product type
options.explanation: Routing helps when inputs need different handling. Here every ad gets the same check.

options.text: Voting: run several independent checks and flag on a set threshold
options.explanation: Correct. Voting runs the same task several times and combines the results, which suits high-stakes checks where a single run is unreliable on borderline cases.

options.text: A single check with a stronger instruction to be careful about minors
options.explanation: One run stays one sample. Stronger wording doesn't remove the variance on borderline ads.

stem: A league's content team turns each game's play-by-play into an English recap, then translates the recap into Spanish. The two steps never change. Now and then the recap step leaves out the final score, and the Spanish version ships with the same gap. Which design best fits?

options.text: Keep the two-step chain and add a programmatic check between the steps that confirms the recap contains the final score and other required fields, retrying or stopping before translation if it doesn't.
options.explanation: Correct. This is prompt chaining with a gate. The steps are fixed, so a workflow fits, and a check between steps catches the defect before it propagates into the translation.

options.text: Replace the pipeline with an autonomous agent that decides on its own when the recap is good enough to translate.
options.explanation: The steps are fixed and known, so an agent adds cost and unpredictability without need. Deterministic checking belongs in code, not in the model's judgment.

options.text: Translate the play-by-play into Spanish first, then write the Spanish recap from the translated play-by-play.
options.explanation: Reordering the steps doesn't add any check, so a recap without the final score can still ship.

options.text: Merge both steps into one prompt that writes the recap and the translation together, so the model sees all the requirements at once.
options.explanation: Merging the steps makes each call harder and removes the point where the output could be checked. The missing score would still slip through.

stem: A platform team's pull-request review pipeline has two needs. First, every PR must be checked against four independent concerns (security, performance, licensing and style), and the review must finish within a minute. Second, for changes that touch authentication, a single vulnerability check sometimes misses real issues, and a missed issue is very costly. Which TWO design choices fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run the vulnerability check once and tell Claude in the prompt that it must be completely certain before passing a change.
options.explanation: Asking for certainty doesn't give independent views of the change. A single run can still miss an issue, which is exactly the failure to address.

options.text: For authentication changes, run the vulnerability check several times in parallel, possibly with different prompts, and flag the PR when the votes cross a threshold set for high recall.
options.explanation: Correct. This is parallelization by voting. Several independent attempts make a miss less likely, which fits a check where false negatives are costly.

options.text: Run four parallel calls, one focused prompt per concern, and aggregate their findings into one review.
options.explanation: Correct. This is parallelization by sectioning: the concerns are independent, focused prompts perform better than one prompt juggling all four, and running them in parallel meets the time limit.

options.text: Use an orchestrator agent that decides at run time which concerns each PR needs, then spawns workers for them.
options.explanation: The four concerns are fixed in advance. Orchestrator-workers fits subtasks that can't be predicted, so here it adds latency and variance for nothing.

options.text: Use one call that reviews all four concerns in sequence within a single prompt, to save tokens.
options.explanation: One prompt covering four concerns divides attention and runs serially, which works against both quality and the one-minute limit.

stem: A stadium's fan-support service gets two kinds of questions: about 90% are simple FAQs (parking, gate times, bag policy) and about 10% are account disputes that need multi-step reasoning over order history. Today one long prompt on an Opus-tier model handles everything, and the FAQ answers come out slow, long and expensive. Which workflow pattern best fits?

options.text: Routing: a classification step sends FAQs to a smaller model with a short FAQ prompt and sends disputes to the more capable model with a dispute-specific prompt.
options.explanation: Correct. The inputs fall into distinct categories that are best handled separately, which is what routing is for. Each path gets its own prompt and a model sized to the task.

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: have a second call critique and refine every answer before it is sent.
options.explanation: Adding a critique loop to every answer increases cost and latency, which are already the problem for the simple FAQs.

options.text: Prompt chaining: run every question through the FAQ prompt first and then through the dispute prompt.
options.explanation: Running every question through both prompts doubles the work. Nothing separates the two kinds of input.

options.text: Orchestrator-workers: split each question into subtasks and delegate them to worker calls.
options.explanation: Most questions are single-step FAQs, so decomposing them adds overhead without benefit.
